name: llm-cliches
title: LLM cliches
description: Stock phrasings and rhythms that language models overproduce. Collected by Simon Willison for the LLM cliche highlighter.

rules.name: “No X, no Y” chains
rules.description: Two or more “no …” items in a row, e.g. “No fluff, no filler, no jargon.” The badge counts the “no” items.
rules.suggest: Say what it does have. A denial chain lists absences instead of substance.

hit: No sign-ups, no downloads, no hassle — just paste and go.
The plan has no hidden fees and no long-term contracts.
No fluff, no filler, no jargon, no corporate buzzwords.
It ships with no bells and whistles, no fluff.
NO FEES, NO CONTRACTS, NO SURPRISES
no fluff; no filler
no time, no money, no way to say no thanks
no-code, no-fuss setup

No fluff, no filler.
No ads here.
miss: There is no catch here, honestly.
No, no, I insist.
no no no
with no list patterns at all, so nothing lights up.
I know nothing, notice nothing.

rules.name: “That’s the whole …”
rules.description: “That / this is the whole point, game, thing …”
rules.suggest: Name the thing directly instead of gesturing at its totality.

hit: That's the whole point.
This is the whole game, really.
That was the whole pitch.
miss: The whole team showed up.

rules.name: “Did not X, did not Y” chains
rules.description: Two or more “did not …” or “didn’t …” items in a row. The badge counts the items.
rules.suggest: Collapse the negations into one concrete statement of what happened.

hit: Did not flinch, did not blink, did not apologize.
He didn't call and didn't write.
Did not know why, did not care.
miss: She did not go.

rules.name: “Don’t VERB it … VERB it”
rules.description: “Don’t call it X. Call it Y.” — a negated verb + “it”, then the same verb + “it” again.
rules.suggest: Drop the setup and keep the reframing, or cut both.

hit: Don't call it a comeback. Call it a return.
Do not think of it as a burden. Think of it as fuel.
Don’t call it "luck." Call it preparation.
Don't just read it — read it aloud.
miss: Don't fear it. Name it.
Don't overthink it.

rules.name: “Sit with that”
rules.description: The reflective “sit with that / this / it (for a moment)”, plus “sit with the discomfort” and friends.
rules.suggest: Say what the reader should conclude, not that they should dwell.

hit: Sit with that for a moment.
Just sit with it.
She was sitting with the discomfort.
miss: Come sit with us at lunch.

rules.name: “You already know”
rules.description: “You already know” — the answer, what to do, or standing alone before a full stop.
rules.suggest: Either state the answer or ask a real question. Do not flatter.

hit: You already know the answer.
Deep down, you already know.
You already know what to do.
Part of you already knows it.
miss: If you already know Python, skip ahead.

rules.name: “Is the entire …”
rules.description: “X is the entire point / game / business model.”
rules.suggest: Replace the totalising claim with the specific mechanism.

hit: Consistency is the entire game.
That's the entire business model.
miss: He toured the entire factory.

rules.name: “The entire … is”
rules.description: “The entire point / game / business model is …” — the flipped twin of “is the entire”.
rules.suggest: Replace the totalising claim with the specific mechanism.

hit: The entire point is that nobody reads.
The entire business model is built on churn.
The entire point of the exercise is repetition.
The entire team was exhausted.
miss: He ate the entire pizza.
The entire history of the modern industrial world economy is complex.

rules.name: “Is real … and / not”
rules.description: “The X is real, and / not …”, including “is the real … and it”. Skips “real estate”, “real time”, and similar.
rules.suggest: Cut "is real". Give the evidence that makes it real.

hit: The improvement is real, and it's not subtle.
This is the real work, and it never ends.
The demand is real and growing.
miss: He is a real estate agent and it shows.
Is it real? And does it matter?
The painting is real, but stolen.

rules.name: “The punchline is”
rules.description: “The punchline is …”, “the punchline:”, or “the punchline?”.
rules.suggest: Deliver the point without announcing that a point is coming.

hit: The punchline is that nobody laughed.
The punchline: nothing changed.
And the punchline? You knew.
miss: He forgot the punchline entirely.

rules.name: “Worth naming”
rules.description: The therapist-voiced “that loss is real and it’s worth naming”, “it’s worth naming that …”, or a “Worth naming:” opener. Skips “naming names”.
rules.suggest: Name it, or cut it. Announcing that something deserves naming is not naming it.

hit: That loss is real and it's worth naming.
It’s worth naming that this hurts.
The grief here is worth naming.
That anger feels worth naming out loud.
Worth naming: nobody asked for this.
miss: It's not worth naming names here.
They spent the meeting naming the new mascot.
The naming convention is worth documenting.

rules.name: “That’s not nothing”
rules.description: “That is not nothing” / “that’s not nothing”, plus the “this / it / which is not nothing” variants.
rules.suggest: Quantify it. "Not nothing" concedes and asserts at once, saying neither.

hit: That's not nothing.
Ten sign-ups in a week — that is not nothing.
It's not nothing, even if it's not everything.
The launch drew a small crowd, which was not nothing.
miss: She insisted that nothing was wrong.
There is nothing left to say.

rules.name: “Is the whole …”
rules.description: Any subject + “is the whole point / trick / pitch / idea”, plus the “here is the whole …” opener. The twin of “is the entire …”, and a generalisation of “That’s the whole …” to subjects other than that/this.
rules.suggest: Name the thing directly instead of gesturing at its totality.

hit: Distribution is the whole game.
Here's the whole pitch in one slide.
That was the whole point of the meeting.
miss: The whole team showed up.

rules.name: Echoing sentence runs
rules.description: Consecutive sentences built on the same repeated skeleton — “A shopping cart is an object in the system. A chat room is an object in the system.” The badge counts the echoing sentences.
rules.suggest: Merge the parallel sentences into one, or vary the structure.

hit: A shopping cart is an object in the system. A chat room is an object in the system.
The parser is a state machine. The renderer is a state machine. The scheduler is a state machine.
miss: The parser is fast today. The renderer is fast today.
The parser is fast. The tests are slow.

rules.name: Performative honesty
rules.description: Sincerity announced rather than demonstrated: “I won’t pretend”, “I’ll be honest”, “let’s be honest”, “to be clear”, and sentence-initial “Honestly,” or “Look,”.
rules.suggest: Delete the preamble. Honest writing does not announce itself.

hit: I won't pretend the migration was painless.
Let's be honest: nobody reads the docs.
To be clear, the API is unchanged.
Honestly, it was fine.
miss: She answered honestly.
Look at the diagram.

rules.name: “That’s the part …”
rules.description: Gesturing at a favoured detail instead of stating it: “that is the part a counter can’t reach”, “the part that makes me trust the rest”, “my favourite part of …”.
rules.suggest: State the detail instead of pointing at it.

hit: That's the part a counter can't reach.
The part that makes me trust the rest is the errata.
My favorite part of the demo was the undo.
miss: He played the part of the villain.

rules.name: “The only X I trust”
rules.description: The narrowing superlative reveal: “the only marketing I trust”, “the only thing it needs”, “the only X that matters”.
rules.suggest: Drop the superlative framing and give the actual reason.

hit: It’s the only marketing I trust.
The only benchmark that matters is retention.
The only thing it needs is a cache.
miss: She was the only engineer on call.

rules.name: “Don’t take my word for it”
rules.description: The stock invitation to verify: “you don’t have to take my word for it”, “don’t take my word for any of this”.
rules.suggest: Just link the evidence.

hit: You don't have to take my word for it.
Don't take my word for any of this.
miss: He kept his word.

rules.name: “Turns out …”
rules.description: The casual-revelation opener, almost always bolted to a tidy conclusion: “Turns out X”, “it turns out that X”.
rules.suggest: State the finding without the casual-reveal framing.

hit: Turns out the cache was never warm.
It turns out that nobody tested it.
miss: She turns out solid work every week.

rules.name: “Fits in your head”
rules.description: Dev-blog boilerplate for simplicity: “small enough to hold in your head”, “batteries included”, “it just works”, “zero config”, “sane defaults”.
rules.suggest: Give the concrete measure - lines of code, number of concepts, setup steps.

hit: The design is small enough to hold in your head.
It ships with sane defaults and zero config.
Install it and it just works.
miss: We choose boring technology on purpose.
The helmet fits your head.

rules.name: Stacked rhetorical questions
rules.description: Two or more questions fired in a row, usually fragments after the first: “Do I know how it works? Where it breaks? Which corners it cut?” The badge counts the questions.
rules.suggest: Keep one question, or convert them to statements.

hit: Do I know how it works? Where it breaks? Which corners it cut?
Was it worth it? Would I do it again?
miss: Did it work? Yes, and then some.
What changed?

rules.name: Repeated sentence openers
rules.description: Three or more consecutive sentences starting on the same word — “Maybe nobody needed it. Maybe it introduced … Maybe a small convenience …” Pronouns and articles are ignored. The badge counts the sentences.
rules.suggest: Vary the sentence openings or combine into one sentence.

hit: Maybe nobody needed it. Maybe the timing was off. Maybe both.
Everything changed. Everything slowed down. Everything cost more.
miss: Maybe nobody needed it. Maybe the timing was off.
The parser is small. The renderer is small. The scheduler is small.

rules.name: Colon into a triple
rules.description: A colon opening onto three or more comma-separated prose items: “separate ports, processes, and local state”. The most common shape LLM prose uses to sound concrete. Tightened from upstream: items must read as prose, not as code, measurements or proper-noun lists.
rules.suggest: Fine in a real list. Suspect when it is prose padding out to three items.

hit: The fix needs three things: separate ports, separate processes, and separate state.
Each service gets its own everything: ports, processes, local state.
It splits into three: the core, the accumulated solver craft, and the agent harness around it.
What it buys: continuous calibration against live data, regression gates on every model edit, and drift alarms that fire early.
miss: The recipe calls for flour, butter, and sugar.
Note: the flag is off by default.
svd_mode: SVD mode ("truncate", "damp", or None).
Returns: theta_opt, cost_history, primary_rms_history.
Chipset: Intel CNVi, hci0, BlueZ 5.
Exit codes: clean, findings over budget, usage/read error.
Reroot k: B=per[k], per[0]=I, per[j]=B-1per[j].
Checks: oracle, gauge-invariance, FK/residual/J parity.
Units: vessels, exchangers, columns, reactors.
Four layers: Frontend Experience, API & Gateway, Cognitive Orchestration, Physical Execution.
The stack: UI, visualization, local SDK in one place.
Pipeline: Perception, Planning, Actuation, Orchestration.
Laptop: Alienware m15 R4, Intel Wi-Fi 6 AX200, Ubuntu 20.
iw shows HE-MCS 11 at 1 Gbps, signal -30 to -40 dBm, 0% packet loss.

rules.name: “Here’s the twist”
rules.description: The stage-managed reveal: “here’s the twist”, “here’s the thing”, “here’s the catch / kicker / rub”, “here’s the first example:”.
rules.suggest: Cut the stage direction and give the content.

hit: Here's the twist: nobody clicked it.
Here is the thing. The demo was fake.
Here's a surprising result: it got faster.
miss: Here's the door code.

rules.name: “X is dead”
rules.description: The obituary headline and its sequel: “peer code review is dead”, “botd is dead; long live botd”.
rules.suggest: Say what changed and for whom, instead of the obituary headline.

hit: Peer code review is dead.
The old importer is dead; long live the importer.
Long live the king.
miss: He played dead until the bear left.

rules.name: “That’s why X mattered”
rules.description: Retroactively assigning significance: “that’s why being able to open the environment mattered”, “this is why preserving every conversation mattered”.
rules.suggest: State the consequence directly rather than asserting significance.

hit: That's why being able to open the environment mattered.
This is why preserving every conversation mattered.
That's why the deadline counts.
miss: That is why we left early.

rules.name: Stranded auxiliary contrast
rules.description: A clause that lands on a bare auxiliary for the reversal: “The tool died; the data didn’t.”, “Reading mostly passed … Writing didn’t”, “Maybe it wouldn’t have.”
rules.suggest: Complete the clause. The bare auxiliary is a rhythm trick, not information.

hit: The tool died; the data didn't.
Reading mostly passed, writing didn't.
Maybe it wouldn't have.
miss: The test passed and the build was green.
